sources.headline: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Airports Prompt Mass Cancellations
sources.text: The Saudi authorities said they intercepted two missiles targeting Riyadh, a day after they said Houthi strikes on airports in the kingdom killed three people.

sources.headline: Flights to Saudi capital suspended after Houthis 'attack on airport'
sources.text: Explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia's capital, including a large blast at Riyadh's international airport, where flights were subsequently halted.

sources.headline: Lufthansa, Air India suspend flights to Riyadh after Houthi attacks
sources.text: Oct 8 - Lufthansa Group airlines and Air India will suspend flights to Riyadh, they said on Thursday, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis renewed threats against airlines after claiming an attack on the Saudi capital's airport.A Lufthansa spokesperson told Reuters the German group's airlines would suspend flights to Riyadh through October 16 due to "current developments in the Middle East". Air India said it had cancelled all flights to the Saudi capital until October 10.Smoke was seen rising from a stationary aircraft at Riyadh airport earlier on Thursday, according to a witness and three people briefed on the matter.The Houthis said they had struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile.Several dozen international flights bound for Riyadh on Thursday evening have been cancelled, data from global flight tracker FlightRadar24 showed.According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, 49.7% of departures from Riyadh airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports. REUTERS

sources.headline: Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks on airports killed three foreign nationals
sources.text: Moroccan, Algerian women killed in Abha, Sudanese national killed in Riyadh.Three civilians have been killed and 36 injured in Houthi-claimed attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday.The attack on Abha International Airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, GACA reported.The attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.GACA said it is working “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities” to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh and destroyed a platform in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.Previous attacks on Saudi airportsNew cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport.On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swathe of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones against Aden airport early on Wednesday. No casualties were reported.Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

sources.headline: Yemen's Houthis claim strikes on Aden, Riyadh airports
sources.text:
Yemen's Houthi rebels attacked an international airport on Wednesday morning, using ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones, according to the Yemeni Ministry of Transport.
Aden International Airport is Yemen's main international gateway outside Houthi control.
The missile reportedly landed near the airport runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, forcing the plane to divert to Jeddah. Two planes on the runway were moved away from the area for fear of further attacks, the Transport Ministry said.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group also attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate confirmation of an attack on the Saudi airport.
Another Houthi ballistic missile was intercepted and destroyed north of Riyadh by the Saudi-led coalition, which said it had tracked the launch to a site in Houthi-controlled Sanaa.
The attacks came as fighting intensified on several fronts in Yemen. Saudi-backed government forces have launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis after the Yemeni insurgent group made territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in recent weeks.Bid for the Red Sea
Government forces, backed by air support from the Saudi-led coalition, launched a lightning offensive to retake territory along the Red Sea coast. The operation succeeded in driving the Houthis out of areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the city of Mocha, which they had seized last month.
In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthi targeted Abha International Airport and an air base in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. It was not immediately clear whether that attack was related to the missile the coalition said it intercepted near Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha International Airport.
Houthis launch airport attacksImage: Saleh Al-Obeidi/AFP
More than 200,000 displaced since fighting began in Yemen, UN agency says
The battle between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis in the country has displaced more than 200,000 people as of Wednesday, according to the latest figures released by the International Organization for Migration.
The UN agency reported the figure to have reached around 76,000 people in mid-September after fighting erupted.
Yemen is experiencing the most serious escalation of fighting and hostilities since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacks in 2022.
